passages.t: Stand firm, and a plea to Euodia and Syntyche
passages.happening:
“Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved” (verse 1).

Then Paul names two women in the church: “I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord” (verse 2). He asks someone he calls “my true yokefellow, to help these women who have labored with me for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Notice how warmly Paul speaks: ‘whom I love and long for, my joy and crown’. A ‘crown’ here is the wreath given to a winner at the games. The Philippians are Paul's prize.

Then, in a letter read aloud to the whole church, Paul names two women who disagree. That would have been a hard moment in the room. But notice how he does it. He does not take sides. He uses the same word, ‘I urge’, for each of them, and he does not tell anyone who was right. He asks them to ‘agree with each other in the Lord’, the same verb for having a mind that he used in 2:2 and 2:5. He wants them to share the mind of Christ.

These were not minor members. They had ‘labored with’ Paul for the gospel, a word for athletes who strive side by side, the same word he used in 1:27. Women had been at the heart of the church in Philippi from its first day, when Lydia and the women at the place of prayer by the river were the first to believe (Acts 16:13-15). Their quarrel mattered because they were leaders.

We do not know who the ‘true yokefellow’ was. Readers have guessed Epaphroditus, Luke, Timothy, or the church as a whole. Clement too is otherwise unknown. What Paul says of them all is enough: their names are in the Book of Life.
passages.ot:
The Book of Life is God's record of his people. Moses prayed for Israel, “if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32). Daniel promised that at the end “everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered” (Daniel 12:1).

And the Psalms sing the goodness of God's people at peace with one another: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.asks: Paul names a quarrel but takes no side, and asks both to share the mind of Christ. If you are at odds with someone in your church or family, ask what it would mean to agree ‘in the Lord’, even before you agree about everything. And if two people near you are at odds, ask whether you could be the ‘true yokefellow’ who helps them.

passages.t: Rejoice, pray instead of worrying, think on what is good
passages.happening:
“Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” (verse 4). “Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near” (verse 5).

“Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (verses 6-7).

“Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable—if anything is excellent or praiseworthy—think on these things” (verse 8). What they have learned and seen in Paul, they are to put into practice, “And the God of peace will be with you” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
‘Rejoice in the Lord always’ is written by a man in chains, waiting for a trial that might end in his death. It is not a call to feel cheerful all the time. It is a call to find joy ‘in the Lord’, who does not change when circumstances do.

‘The Lord is near’ can mean near in place, close beside you, or near in time, coming soon. Both are true, and both give a reason not to be ruled by worry.

Notice that Paul does not simply say ‘stop worrying’. He says what to do instead: bring everything to God, by prayer, by asking, and with thanks. And notice what he promises. Not that every request will be granted as asked, but that God's peace will ‘guard’ the heart and mind. ‘Guard’ is a soldier's word. The Philippians lived in a city with Roman soldiers, and Paul himself was guarded by soldiers. He says God's peace will stand guard over them.

Verse 8 reads like the lists of virtues the moral teachers of the day made. Paul tells believers to fill their minds with whatever is true and good, wherever they find it. And then, verse 9, to do it, not only think it.
passages.ot:
The Psalms invite God's people to bring their burdens to him: “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you” (Psalm 55:22). “The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth” (Psalm 145:18).

Isaiah promises peace to the mind that rests on God: “You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You” (Isaiah 26:3).

And Habakkuk shows joy in the Lord when everything else has failed: “Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines” and the fields produce nothing, “yet I will exult in the LORD” (Habakkuk 3:17-18).
passages.hard:
‘Be anxious for nothing.’ Does this mean that a believer who feels anxious has failed?

No. This verse is sometimes used as if anxiety were a switch a faithful person can simply turn off, so that anyone who still feels anxious has failed, or is told that prayer should replace a doctor. That is not what Paul says. He gives a practice, not a switch: bring everything to God in prayer, with thanks. He promises God's peace, not that every request will be granted as asked. And Paul himself admits to sorrow and to being anxious (2:27-28) and to the daily pressure of his care for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). The verse calls a worried person toward God. It does not shame them for being worried.

This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you are anxious about today, and whether you have told God about it, plainly and specifically, with thanks for what he has already done. Ask what your mind dwells on most of the day, and whether it is true, right and good. And if worry has become more than you can carry, ask who you could tell this week.

passages.happening:
Paul thanks them: “Now I rejoice greatly in the Lord that at last you have revived your concern for me” (verse 10). But he is careful: “I am not saying this out of need, for I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances” (verse 11).

“I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. I am accustomed to any and every situation—to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need” (verse 12). “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (verse 13).

“Nevertheless, you have done well to share in my affliction” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The word for ‘content’ was a favourite of the Stoic teachers of Paul's day. They taught that a wise person should need nothing outside himself, and should be the same whatever happened. Paul uses their word but changes its source. His contentment does not come from needing nothing. It comes from Christ, who strengthens him.

‘I am accustomed’ (verse 12) translates a word used for being let in on a secret, as in the secret rites of some religions of the time. Paul says he has been let in on the secret of being content: it is Christ.

And look at what he has learned to be content in. Not only plenty, but hunger. Not only abundance, but need. Some people find it harder to be content with too much than with too little. Paul has learned both.

Then comes verse 13. In its place it is not about winning games, getting rich or reaching every goal. It is about going hungry without despair, and having plenty without pride, because Christ gives the strength to do both.

Notice too that Paul does not pretend he was fine alone. ‘You have done well to share in my affliction.’ Contentment in Christ and gratitude for friends go together.
passages.ot:
Israel learned in the wilderness that life depends on God, not on full barns: “in your hunger He gave you manna to eat”, Moses said, “so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Proverbs prays for the contentment Paul learned: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion. Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You, saying, ‘Who is the LORD?’ Or I may become poor and steal” (Proverbs 30:8-9).

And the shepherd psalm says it in one line: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1).
passages.hard:
‘I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.’ Does this mean God will help me do anything I set my mind to?

This verse is printed on sports shirts and wristbands and quoted before games and job interviews. Read in its place, it says something harder and better. Paul wrote it from prison, not from a stage. The ‘all things’ are the things he has just named: being filled and being hungry, having plenty and having need. The strength Christ gives him is the strength to be content, to go hungry without despair and to have plenty without pride.

So the verse is not a slogan for ambition, and it is not a promise that faith will bring success. It is a prisoner's peace. A person who has lost a job, a game, their health or their plans can still say it, and say it truly, because it was first said by a man who had lost his freedom.

It can rightly give courage for hard things God asks of us. But it promises Christ's strength in every circumstance, not a change of circumstance. The site's guide ‘What Does Philippians 4:13 Really Mean?’ says more.
passages.asks: Ask where you are least content: in need, or in plenty. Ask whether you have used this verse as a promise of success, and what it would mean to use it instead as a prayer for contentment. And ask whom you could thank, as Paul did, for sharing in your hard times.

passages.t: A gift like a sacrifice, and a promise for needs
passages.happening:
Paul remembers their history: when he left Macedonia, “no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (verse 15). “For even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again” (verse 16).

“Not that I am seeking a gift” (verse 17). “I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus. They are a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God” (verse 18).

“And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus. To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen” (verses 19-20).

Greetings follow, “especially those from the household of Caesar” (verse 22), and a blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
In the Greek and Roman world, gifts between friends came with strings. A gift put the receiver in debt, and he was expected to give something back. That may be why Paul thanks them so carefully. He does not want them to think he is hinting for more, and he does not want to be in anyone's debt but God's. So he calls their gift an offering to God: ‘a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice’. What they gave Paul, they gave to God.

‘The household of Caesar’ did not mean the emperor's family. It meant the large staff of slaves and freed slaves who served the emperor's government, many in responsible posts, in Rome and in the provinces. Some of them had become believers. The gospel had reached into the heart of the empire's service.

And notice who receives the promise of verse 19. It is a church that had given again and again, often out of its own poverty, as Paul says elsewhere of the churches of Macedonia (2 Corinthians 8:1-2). Paul says that the God who received their gift will meet their needs.
passages.ot:
A gift given to God's servant becomes an offering to God, like the sacrifices of Israel: “a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma” (Exodus 29:18).

The promise that God provides goes back to Abraham on the mountain: “And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14). And the law joined generosity with God's care: “Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so” (Deuteronomy 15:10).

The Psalms say it simply: “those who seek the LORD lack no good thing” (Psalm 34:10).
passages.hard:
‘My God will supply all your needs.’ Is this a promise that God will make believers rich if they give?

No. Some teachers use this verse, with others, to promise health and wealth in return for faith or giving. That teaching is an error, and it misreads this letter badly. Paul writes these words in chains, just after saying he has known hunger and need (verse 12). The promise is for ‘needs’, not wants, and it is made to a church that had given out of its own poverty, not as an investment. It is a promise that God will care for his people, not a contract that pays a return.

God's ‘glorious riches in Christ Jesus’ are the riches of his grace, given in Christ. Sometimes God meets needs through other people, as he met Paul's through the Philippians.

If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul calls the Philippians' gift a sacrifice that pleased God. Ask whom you could help this week, and whether you would see it as an offering to God. Ask whether you trust God to meet your needs, or keep reaching for more than you need. And let the letter end with you as it ends: with grace.
